extracted.intended_audience: Federal agencies, State and Tribal conservation agencies, resource managers, landowners, conservation organizations, and public commenters on ESA listing actions
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register proposed listing determination for the Santa Ana speckled dace including the proposed section 4(d) protective regulations, analysis of status and significant-portion-of-range, critical habitat determinability, recovery planning, and interagency consultation requirements. The page provides legal standards, procedural rules, exceptions, and criteria the Service uses in these determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant portion of range (SPR) analysis approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus analysis on portions of the species' range that may meet the Act's definition of an endangered species by determining whether threats or their effects on the species are greater in any biologically meaningful portion of the species' range than in other portions such that the species is currently in danger of extinction in that portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a negative answer is reached for the first question (whether a portion is in danger of extinction), no need to evaluate the other question for that portion. The range can be divided many ways; the Service focuses on biologically meaningful portions and considers threats, effects, and differences in biological condition across portions when deciding SPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate specific threats affecting the species, including habitat loss, habitat degradation, habitat fragmentation, increased risk of wildfire, changing climate trends, nonnative species, and small population effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether these threats are concentrated or more severe in particular analysis units; use best available scientific and commercial information to evaluate current condition and how threats influence extinction risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis-unit assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating portions of range (analysis units), assess unit-specific metrics including number of occupied occurrences, amount of occupied habitat (stream miles), habitat availability, habitat quality, connectivity, and population size/abundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from this analysis: rated availability as 'low' where under 20 stream miles of occupied habitat that do not require management; habitat quality judged by presence of essential features (habitat free of nonnative species, adequate flows, appropriate water quality, proper substrate); connectivity rated by ability to disperse between extant and historically occupied sites; population size judged from known extant occurrences and flow-dependent abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining significance of a portion
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether a portion is 'significant' by evaluating its geographic size relative to rest of range, proportion of occurrences and occupied river miles it contains, whether it is spatially disjunct, and whether it may contain unique genetic or biological attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective and individual significance considered; small geographic area or low proportion of occurrences/river miles argues against significance, but uniqueness (e.g., unique alleles, disjunct Tribal lands) can support significance even if area or percentage is small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing determination standard (threatened vs endangered)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use best available scientific and commercial information to determine whether the species meets the Act's definitions: 'endangered' (in danger of extinction now) or 'threatened' (likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite sections 3(20) and 4(a)(1) of the Act; explain conclusions transparently; example conclusion here: Santa Ana speckled dace proposed as 'threatened' based on the described threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available conservation measures upon listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing provides recognition, planning and implementation of recovery actions, Federal protection requirements, and prohibitions against certain practices; encourages cooperation among Federal, State, Tribal, local, private, and international partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery planning (outlines, teams, criteria, monitoring, cost estimates), recovery actions (habitat restoration, research, captive propagation, outreach), and funding sources (Federal budgets, State programs, section 6 grants, cost-share programs) are described; recovery outlines/drafts/final plans will be made publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery planning process requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(f) requires development and implementation of recovery plans to restore listed species to secure, self-sustaining conditions; begins with a recovery outline available after final listing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recovery teams and identification of actions necessary to halt/reverse decline; recovery plans include recovery criteria for downlisting/delisting and monitoring methods; plans can be revised as new substantive information becomes available; coordination framework and cost estimates should be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 7 interagency consultation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 mandates Federal action agencies use existing authorities to further conservation and ensure actions they authorize, fund, or carry out are not likely to jeopardize listed species or adversely modify designated critical habitat; formal consultation is required when actions may affect listed species/critical habitat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal agencies must review actions early and consult per 50 CFR part 402; informal concurrence covers 'not likely to adversely affect' (requires Service's written concurrence); formal consultation results in a biological opinion. Section 7(a)(4) requires conference for actions likely to jeopardize proposed species or proposed critical habitat; processes are the same regardless of 4(d) rules. Tools to streamline consultation (guidance, IPC keys, templates, programmatic consultations) may be developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and authority of Section 4(d) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4(d) authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations deemed necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of threatened species and to include among those regulations any prohibitions under section 9 applicable to endangered species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have recognized broad Secretary discretion; 4(d) rules are species-specific tools and do not alter recovery planning or section 7 consultation requirements; the Service may explain how a proposed suite of prohibitions/exceptions satisfies the 'necessary and advisable' criterion for conservation even when not required to make a separate determination for each section 9 prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions incorporated into the proposed 4(d) rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed 4(d) rule incorporates section 9(a)(1) prohibitions (as implemented at 50 CFR 17.21) making it illegal to import/export, take, possess/sell/transport unlawfully taken specimens, engage in commerce-related transport/delivery, or sell/offer for sale in interstate/foreign commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'take' per the Act (harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap, capture, collect, or attempt) and cites 50 CFR 17.3 for further definitions; prohibits take except for actions and activities specifically excepted by the 4(d) rule; emphasizes conservation rationale for prohibitions (prevent further declines, preserve populations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permits and statutory exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits may be issued to authorize otherwise-prohibited activities for scientific purposes, to enhance propagation or survival, economic hardship, zoological exhibition, educational purposes, incidental taking, or special purposes consistent with the Act (50 CFR 17.32); sections 9 and 10 also contain statutory exemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees/agents of Federal agencies, State conservation agencies with cooperative agreements, Tribes, etc., may take threatened wildlife without a permit when acting in official duties for specified purposes (aid sick/injured/orphaned, dispose/salvage dead specimens, remove specimens posing demonstrable but nonimmediate human safety threats under humane conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-specific incidental take exceptions under 4(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed 4(d) rule excepts incidental take from certain activities expected to be negligible or beneficial: (1) forest/wildland management activities intended to minimize rangewide negative impacts and maintain defensible space to reduce wildfire risk; (2) habitat restoration/enhancement activities in nonpermitted Federal or State plans that benefit the species; and (3) removal of nonnative species (plants and aquatic predators) for species benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excepted activities should be intended to reduce wildfire risk or improve habitat and are expected to have negligible or beneficial impacts. Habitat restoration examples: trash removal, dam removal, restoration from recreational mining, beneficial dam operations in a Service-approved plan. Nonnative species removal may include mechanical/chemical control consistent with law and eradication of nonnative animals (catfish, bass, crayfish, bullfrogs); electrofishing for eradication requires prior Service approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical habitat definition and designation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical habitat includes specific areas within the geographical area occupied at listing that contain physical/biological features essential to conservation and that may require special management, and specific areas outside the occupied area determined essential for conservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the first prong, designations identify, to the extent known using best scientific data available, the essential physical/biological features (space, food, cover, protected habitat). Under the second prong, unoccupied areas may be designated if essential. Use the SSA report, recovery plan, peer-reviewed literature, state/county conservation plans, surveys, biological assessments, unpublished materials, and expert opinion as information sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best available scientific data and information quality standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 requires designating critical habitat on the basis of the best scientific data available; the Service's Information Standards policy and Information Quality Act/Guidelines require use of primary and original sources when consistent with the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biologists must use primary/original information to the extent consistent with the Act and best available scientific data standards; decisions should be transparent and supported by cited sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical habitat determinability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical habitat is 'not determinable' under 50 CFR 424.12(a)(2) when (i) data sufficient to perform required analyses are lacking, or (ii) the biological needs of the species are not sufficiently well known to identify any area meeting the definition of critical habitat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If determinability is lacking (e.g., pending complex economic impact assessment or insufficient biological data), the Service may conclude designation not determinable at listing and may take up to an additional year to publish critical habitat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and plain-language requirements for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: By E.O.s 12866 and 12988 and Presidential Memorandum, rules must be written in plain language and meet specified clarity criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each rule must: (1) be logically organized; (2) use active voice to address readers directly; (3) use clear language rather than jargon; (4) be divided into short sections and sentences; and (5) use lists and tables wherever possible. The Service requests specific comments if these requirements are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of State and Tribal partners and section 6 cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Service must cooperate with States to the maximum extent practicable under section 6; State agencies with cooperative agreements may have designated employees/agents able to carry out actions that may result in otherwise-prohibited take when conducted to conserve the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State agencies often possess valuable data/expertise and close relationships with local governments and landowners; cooperative agreements under section 6(c) enable qualified State employees/agents to conduct conservation activities without additional authorization when designated.
